questions.title: A decision that the pilot can actually answer
questions.stem: A manufacturer wants to decide whether an assistant reduces engineer investigation time enough to justify integration. Historical tickets include only resolved incidents; difficult abandoned investigations were never recorded. The prototype performs well on those historical tickets. A six-week pilot can observe live investigations but cannot change safety approvals. Which pilot scope BEST produces a credible business decision rather than merely reproducing the favorable demonstration?

options.text: Deploy on historical resolved tickets only and extrapolate the demonstrated reduction to all live investigations, retaining existing safety approvals and planned integration scope.
options.why: The resolved-only sample excludes the cases most likely to change the business estimate.

options.text: Observe representative live investigations, including abandonment and review effort, compare against a defined baseline, and retain existing safety approvals during the pilot.
options.why: It measures the intended time outcome on the missing real-workload cases without altering safety authority.

options.text: Deploy to volunteer expert engineers and measure draft generation speed, using their satisfaction to infer total investigation time across the engineering organization.
options.why: Expert volunteers and generation speed do not establish representative investigation-time benefit.

options.text: Begin broad integration while recording safety approvals, postponing investigation-time measurement until enough completed incidents accumulate after the production launch.
options.why: It commits to integration before collecting the evidence needed for that business decision.

questions.decision: The pilot must test the business hypothesis on the missing workload and full human effort, not only repeat a selectively successful technical demonstration.

questions.title: Outcome feedback without live learning
questions.stem: A transport assistant suggests alternate delivery windows when a depot is congested. Dispatchers may accept or edit the suggestions, and bookings occur in a separate system. The prototype logs excellent suggestion ratings, yet managers cannot determine whether detention charges fall. Privacy rules permit pseudonymous shipment linkage for thirty days. Which TWO changes most directly create an accountable architecture that can establish business impact?

options.text: Join versioned suggestions and dispatcher decisions to final shipment outcomes using the permitted linkage, including detention charges and unsuccessful scheduling attempts.
options.why: It connects advice to the downstream outcome, including failures that ratings alone miss.

options.text: Increase the allowed retention of raw dispatcher conversations and compare monthly suggestion counts against the total number of depot visits.
options.why: More raw data and counts do not create the required suggestion-to-outcome linkage.

options.text: Assign an operations owner to review outcome slices, select regression cases, and approve measured scheduling changes before each controlled release.
options.why: An owner converts outcome evidence into accountable changes rather than uncontrolled feedback ingestion.

options.text: Replace dispatcher ratings with an automatic model judge scoring how persuasive each alternative delivery window sounds to the recipient.
options.why: Persuasiveness does not establish reduced charges or improved actual scheduling outcomes.

options.text: Train the next prompt automatically on accepted suggestions each night, using the existing dispatcher approval as sufficient correctness labeling.
options.why: Acceptance is not proven downstream success; unreviewed updates also weaken release accountability.

questions.decision: The architectural gap is a measured output-to-outcome loop plus an owner who can safely act on it, within the stated retention boundary.

questions.title: When a bounded agent is justified
questions.stem: A research team investigates novel material failures. Each observation determines which laboratory records or literature to inspect next, and the number of branches is unpredictable. A fixed workflow now contains hundreds of brittle branches and repeatedly stops on new evidence patterns. The team permits read-only exploration, requires cited findings, and imposes a strict work budget. Which architecture BEST fits these conditions while preserving accountable termination?

options.text: Use a read-only investigative agent with cited findings and a separate budget for each new branch, permitting unlimited branch creation until findings converge.
options.why: Per-branch limits do not enforce the strict total work budget when the number of branches is unpredictable.

options.text: Use a bounded investigative agent with approved read tools, explicit evidence contracts, budget and stopping rules, and escalation when uncertainty remains.
options.why: Adaptive branching is genuinely needed; bounded tools and stopping rules preserve the stated scope and resource limits.

options.text: Prefetch a fixed evidence packet for one augmented-model call, escalating every unanticipated record need to researchers rather than allowing further read-only exploration.
options.why: A fixed packet turns the recurring unpredictable evidence needs into avoidable manual interruptions instead of supporting bounded exploration.

options.text: Maintain explicit workflow branches with model-selected parameters, adding each newly observed evidence pattern to the documented branch catalog before automated continuation.
options.why: It keeps the demonstrated brittle enumeration requirement even though evidence-dependent branch structure is unpredictable.

questions.decision: Variable input alone does not justify autonomy, but demonstrated unpredictable evidence-dependent exploration can; retain bounded authority, evidence, and termination contracts.

questions.title: Parallel analysis with controlled synthesis
questions.stem: A merger-review team needs independent analyses of competition, contract obligations, and data migration. Each specialist can read a different approved corpus; no specialist may access another corpus directly. Their conclusions sometimes conflict because entities use different identifiers. The final recommendation must expose unresolved conflicts and stay within an execution budget. Which THREE orchestration choices BEST preserve useful independence while producing an auditable final synthesis?

options.text: Ask three identical generalist agents to vote on the combined report after loading all corpora into their shared context.
options.why: Shared unrestricted corpora violate access constraints and voting does not resolve mismatched identifiers.

options.text: Require the coordinator to reconcile identifier mappings and display incompatible findings with provenance instead of silently choosing the majority conclusion.
options.why: Conflicting entity interpretations require explicit resolution or escalation, not ungrounded consensus.

options.text: Bound specialist retries and total work, returning a partial report with missing analyses when the budget prevents complete synthesis.
options.why: A bounded partial report preserves budget and makes coverage gaps visible.

options.text: Allow specialists to exchange unrestricted corpus excerpts directly whenever they disagree, keeping the coordinator limited to final formatting work.
options.why: Direct exchange violates the stated corpus access boundary despite potentially faster reconciliation.

options.text: Give each specialist a scoped task contract with entity identifiers, evidence references, uncertainty fields, and only its approved corpus access.
options.why: Contracts let independent results be compared without granting unnecessary cross-corpus access.

questions.decision: Parallelize independent expertise, standardize the evidence interface, and retain explicit reconciliation and resource boundaries at the coordinator.

questions.title: Decomposition that preserves dependencies
questions.stem: A rail-maintenance planner must recommend work packages from inspection narratives, available crews, and track-access windows. The model can summarize each input well, but its combined plans assign crews to overlapping locations. Access and crew constraints are available as structured data and must be satisfied exactly. Which decomposition BEST improves reliability while retaining Claude for the parts that require interpreting unstructured inspection findings?

options.text: Have separate crew and access agents create locally valid plans, then ask a writing agent to merge their recommendations into one readable schedule.
options.why: Independently valid plans can conflict jointly; a writing merge does not enforce coupled constraints.

options.text: Generate three complete plans with a more capable model and select the plan that an independent language-model judge considers most coherent.
options.why: Coherence voting cannot establish exact nonoverlap when structured validation is available.

options.text: Split the inspection narrative into equal token segments and combine each segment’s recommended work package in the original report order.
options.why: Token boundaries ignore shared crews and track windows, retaining the underlying global conflict.

options.text: Extract inspection needs with evidence, validate resource constraints in a deterministic scheduler, then have Claude explain the feasible plan and unresolved exceptions.
options.why: It separates interpretation from exact joint constraint solving and explains only validated feasible plans.

questions.decision: Decomposition must preserve the dependencies that make a solution valid; exact cross-task constraints belong in an explicit validation or solving step.

questions.title: Capacity savings after review cost
questions.stem: A claims team handles 6,000 cases per month. Each currently needs twelve staff minutes. A controlled pilot reduces preparation to four minutes but adds two minutes of verification; all other work is unchanged. The manager wants the monthly capacity gain before considering staffing decisions. Assume the same case volume, no rework change, and sixty minutes per staff hour. Which interpretation is BEST supported?

options.text: The pilot releases 800 staff hours monthly; verification remains an existing oversight responsibility and should therefore be excluded from the calculation.
options.why: Verification is explicitly added by the pilot; excluding it overstates capacity gain by 200 hours.

options.text: The pilot releases 1,200 staff hours monthly; preparation is automated, so the existing case-handling baseline becomes the full available capacity.
options.why: Four preparation and two verification minutes remain for every case, so the full baseline is not released.

options.text: The pilot releases 600 staff hours monthly; whether this produces cash savings depends on staffing, demand, redeployment, and implementation costs.
options.why: Net saving is six minutes per case, totaling 36,000 minutes or 600 hours; cash savings are not automatic.

options.text: The pilot releases 600 staff hours monthly; monthly payroll should fall by the equivalent amount once the pilot reaches the stated volume.
options.why: The capacity arithmetic is right, but payroll reduction requires a staffing or expenditure change not supplied.

questions.decision: Count all changed human work before estimating benefit. Six thousand times six minutes divided by sixty is 600 hours; capacity is distinct from cash.

questions.title: When a useful non-agent answer wins
questions.stem: A regional insurer wants an assistant to answer questions about four approved product leaflets totaling 9,000 tokens. The leaflets change twice yearly, fit comfortably in the available context, and have identical access rights. Pilot answers with supplied leaflets meet quality and response targets. No external actions or live prices are needed. Which TWO design choices BEST fit the evidence and keep future change manageable?

options.text: Attach product-update and customer-record tools now so the same assistant can support future transactional product changes without redesigning its interface.
options.why: Unused transactional authority expands scope and attack surface beyond the approved question-answering task.

options.text: Record the tested document and prompt versions with acceptance cases, revisiting retrieval when corpus size, access boundaries, or freshness requirements change.
options.why: Versioning supports safe maintenance and defines concrete triggers for revisiting the simpler architecture.

options.text: Introduce a research agent with web search so it can supplement approved leaflets whenever its confidence in a policy answer is low.
options.why: Unapproved outside material changes the evidence boundary despite no current information gap requiring web research.

options.text: Create an embedding index immediately and require every answer to use retrieved snippets, even when the complete approved material fits efficiently.
options.why: Retrieval adds a new failure surface without a demonstrated need or benefit under the stated pilot evidence.

options.text: Begin with an augmented Claude call using versioned approved leaflets, explicit citation requirements, and an abstention rule for unsupported product details.
options.why: The measured context-based approach satisfies current needs without an unnecessary retrieval or action layer.

questions.decision: Choose the simplest architecture demonstrated to meet requirements, but preserve versioned evidence and specific conditions under which the decision should change.

questions.title: A correlated consensus failure
questions.stem: Three agents independently review a subsidy application, and a coordinator approves whenever two agree. All three use the same retrieved eligibility excerpt. A truncation bug removes its exception clause, and every agent recommends the wrong action with consistent explanations. Management asks for the smallest architectural correction that addresses this demonstrated failure without multiplying routine processing cost. Which change is BEST?

options.text: Randomize each reviewer’s wording and temperature, then keep the majority rule so the resulting opinions are less linguistically similar.
options.why: Different wording does not restore the missing exception or establish independent evidence.

options.text: Add two more reviewers using the same excerpt and require four agreeing recommendations before the coordinator approves an application.
options.why: More votes on the same incomplete evidence preserve the correlated failure and increase routine cost.

options.text: Retain the current reviews but ask the coordinator to rewrite minority concerns more prominently in the final approval rationale.
options.why: There was no informed minority; formatting cannot create evidence that every reviewer lacked.

options.text: Validate required eligibility evidence before review and route missing or contradictory clauses to an exception path before approval.
options.why: The shared missing evidence is the causal failure; gating completeness addresses it before correlated decisions occur.

questions.decision: Multiple model calls are not independent safeguards when they share the same defective evidence. Repair the common dependency.

questions.title: A recoverable external effect
questions.stem: A conference assistant drafts speaker invitations, obtains organizer approval, then calls a mail service. The service sometimes times out after accepting the message, and a retry can send a duplicate invitation. The organizer must retain authority over wording and recipient changes. Which TWO changes BEST make the end-to-end architecture recoverable without discarding the approved draft whenever a transient network failure occurs?

options.text: Bind approval to the draft version and recipient, requiring renewed approval for material changes while permitting safe retries of the same operation.
options.why: It preserves organizer authority without treating an unchanged transport retry as a new content decision.

options.text: Suppress all retries permanently and report every mail timeout as an unsuccessful send, relying on organizers to send another invitation manually.
options.why: It can trigger duplicate manual sends and falsely labels an uncertain external outcome as definite failure.

options.text: Generate a fresh invitation and identifier for each retry, assuming the organizer’s initial approval covers the same overall communication goal.
options.why: Fresh identifiers defeat deduplication, and changed wording is not the approved content.

options.text: Persist the approved invitation and an operation identifier, then use an idempotent send interface or reconcile delivery state before retrying.
options.why: A durable operation identity prevents blind duplicate effects when timeout leaves the outcome uncertain.

options.text: Ask Claude to inspect its previous explanation after a timeout and infer whether the mail service probably accepted the invitation.
options.why: Language-model inference is not evidence of the external service’s committed delivery state.

questions.decision: Separate approved intent, durable execution identity, and uncertain external outcome. Recovery should reconcile state rather than recreate intent.

questions.title: Accuracy gates before a cheaper cascade
questions.stem: A multilingual service compares three fictional routing designs on the same held-out workload. Every released language must achieve at least 95% correct routing; p95 completion must stay below three seconds. Cost is minimized after those gates. The proposed cascade uses a small model on easy cases and a larger model on exceptions. The exhibit reports measured system results, including routing overhead. Which initial release choice is BEST justified?

options.text: Choose the large single-model design because its superior correctness is worth the added cost even after all stated release gates pass.
options.why: Extra correctness has no stated priority after the gates; balanced meets them more cheaply.

options.text: Choose the balanced single-model design because it passes every language gate and latency limit at the lowest cost among feasible candidates.
options.why: The cascade fails the minority-language gate; the larger single model is feasible but costs more than balanced.

options.text: Choose the cascade for all languages, increasing the escalation threshold until its minority-language accuracy is assumed to match the balanced model.
options.why: A threshold hypothesis needs measurement; assumed slice improvement does not establish release readiness.

options.text: Choose the cascade because its pooled accuracy exceeds the requirement and its measured cost is lowest across the representative workload.
options.why: The requirement applies to each language, so the pooled result cannot conceal the failing language slice.

questions.decision: Apply the actual slice-level quality gate before optimizing cost. A well-designed cascade remains a candidate until its measured weaknesses are repaired.

questions.title: Partitioning an evidence-heavy investigation
questions.stem: A procurement investigator must compare several thousand supplier disclosures with contract obligations. Individual documents fit context, but the entire corpus does not. A single summarization chain loses minority findings, and the final recommendation must cite every material discrepancy. Work can run asynchronously, but the system may not treat absence from a summary as proof that no discrepancy exists. Which design is BEST?

options.text: Summarize each document to a fixed paragraph and repeatedly summarize the paragraphs until the entire corpus fits the final recommendation context.
options.why: Repeated compression can erase minority discrepancies and lacks explicit coverage or evidence-preservation guarantees.

options.text: Sample the longest supplier disclosures first and stop when the recommendation context fills, marking unsampled suppliers as having no identified discrepancies.
options.why: Unsampled material has not been reviewed; the proposal violates the requirement about unsupported absence.

options.text: Use one agent with a larger output allowance to inspect documents sequentially, carrying forward only its current recommendation and confidence estimate.
options.why: A current narrative and confidence estimate do not preserve traceable findings or coverage across thousands of documents.

options.text: Partition by explicit obligation and supplier, extract source-linked findings with coverage records, then reconcile cross-partition discrepancies before producing the recommendation.
options.why: Obligation-based partitioning and coverage records retain evidence and expose unreviewed areas instead of equating omission with absence.

questions.decision: Decompose around the comparison unit and preserve both positive findings and coverage evidence; summaries alone are not a completeness mechanism.

questions.title: The model route must be measurable
questions.stem: A service can route routine classification to a cheaper model and difficult classification to a larger one. The routing model labels 30% of requests difficult. A pilot evaluates only the difficult requests and reports excellent accuracy, while finance assumes the remaining requests are equally accurate. The business requires at least 96% end-to-end correctness across the production mix. Which next step BEST supports a defensible model decision?

options.text: Deploy the cascade because the larger model passes the difficult-case benchmark and the cheaper model receives requests labeled easier by design.
options.why: A label of easier is not evidence that the cheaper path meets the required quality.

options.text: Evaluate the full routing system on a held-out production mix, including incorrectly routed cases, escalation overhead, and quality within important slices.
options.why: End-to-end evaluation includes the untested easy path and routing mistakes that could invalidate the business gate.

options.text: Compare the two models only on difficult requests and route all remaining cases by whichever model has lower published input pricing.
options.why: Difficult-only testing cannot establish accuracy for the majority path; unit pricing omits routing overhead.

options.text: Raise the difficult-request share to fifty percent and assume the added larger-model coverage guarantees the required end-to-end correctness.
options.why: More escalation may help, but an arbitrary fraction does not prove the required system result.

questions.decision: A model-routing architecture includes the router and every downstream path; measure the complete system rather than its best-tested component.

questions.title: Examples disagree with the policy
questions.stem: A Claude assistant classifies export requests. Its versioned policy says ambiguous destinations require escalation, but old few-shot examples approve similar ambiguous destinations. Reviewers find inconsistent outputs despite a clear output schema. The business needs a reliable repair and evidence that routine classifications still work. Which TWO actions BEST address the conflict without treating the examples as authoritative replacements for policy?

options.text: Add ambiguous-destination and routine cases to a held-out regression suite, checking escalation behavior as well as schema validity after the change.
options.why: The test checks the actual policy behavior and prevents a fix from degrading routine cases.

options.text: Have the model explain which example it trusted for each decision, using explanation fluency as the release criterion for the updated prompt.
options.why: An articulate explanation can justify the wrong policy and is not evidence of correct escalation behavior.

options.text: Remove or correct examples that contradict the approved policy, and clearly separate task instructions from request content in the revised prompt.
options.why: Contradictory examples create competing behavioral guidance; alignment and separation address that prompt-level cause.

options.text: Move the contradictory examples earlier in the prompt so the model has more space to reconcile them before reading the current policy.
options.why: Reordering does not eliminate the policy contradiction or establish the intended authoritative behavior.

options.text: Constrain the schema to approval and rejection values, removing escalation so the model cannot produce an inconsistent intermediate classification.
options.why: It removes the expressly required ambiguous-case escalation and sacrifices semantic correctness for schema consistency.

questions.decision: Resolve inconsistent guidance and test the targeted behavior. Valid structure and fluent explanations do not establish compliance with the approved policy.

questions.title: Compact the history without rewriting authority
questions.stem: A long-running account research session approaches its context limit. It contains obsolete search results, current customer constraints, approved evidence links, and one unresolved legal restriction. The assistant has begun overlooking that restriction after several summarization cycles. Tools can retrieve historical evidence when needed, but changing the restriction requires a separate authorized decision. Which context-management strategy BEST preserves the information needed for correct continuation?

options.text: Increase output tokens so the assistant can restate more of the history in every reply before continuing its account investigation.
options.why: More output consumes budget and does not establish faithful retention of the critical restriction.

options.text: Discard all earlier messages once the latest user request fits the window, assuming important restrictions will be restated when needed.
options.why: The unresolved restriction remains binding even when the latest request does not repeat it.

options.text: Summarize the entire history into a short persuasive narrative and treat the newest summary as the sole authority for the remaining session.
options.why: A narrative can silently omit restrictions and makes accumulated compression the authority instead of approved source decisions.

options.text: Preserve authoritative constraints, open decisions, and evidence references in validated current-state records; compact obsolete details into retrievable history.
options.why: It distinguishes durable authority and open decisions from disposable history, while preserving evidence access and checking compaction fidelity.

questions.decision: Compaction should preserve explicit current constraints and provenance, with checks for lost authority; chronology and narrative smoothness are secondary.

questions.title: Correct ordering but inconsistent tool schemas
questions.stem: A team already places stable tools and policy before dynamic case text. Its eligible prefix exceeds the supplied model minimum; requests arrive every minute within a five-minute cache lifetime. Cache writes remain frequent. Traces show generated descriptions of the same tools vary on every request, while policy and tool behavior are unchanged. Which TWO actions BEST target the demonstrated miss cause without changing supported capabilities?

options.text: Replace tool schemas with names alone so the prefix becomes stable, asking Claude to infer the required argument structures from previous calls.
options.why: It removes the registered execution contract and compromises supported tool behavior to improve cache metrics.

options.text: Canonicalize and version the semantically unchanged tool definitions so repeated requests use identical schema and description bytes before the policy prefix.
options.why: Tool definitions precede policy in the cached prefix; unnecessary textual variation breaks exact prefix reuse.

options.text: Replay requests with fixed tool definitions and compare cache reads and writes, while checking selection accuracy and preserving intentionally changed tool versions.
options.why: A controlled replay tests the identified variable and ensures optimization does not freeze legitimate capability changes.

options.text: Increase the cache lifetime while preserving minute-by-minute schema variation, treating lifetime as the only remaining reason eligible prefixes can miss.
options.why: Requests already arrive within the stated lifetime; different prefix bytes remain a separate invalidation cause.

options.text: Move dynamic case text farther after the policy while retaining newly generated tool descriptions, assuming additional separation restores prefix identity.
options.why: The varying tool definitions still occur before the reusable policy, so later dynamic placement does not fix the mismatch.

questions.decision: Cache eligibility and ordering are necessary but insufficient: exact stable bytes include tool definitions before policy. Isolate changed prefix material with telemetry.

questions.title: Reasoning detail has a cost
questions.stem: A contract assistant produces a risk label, short cited justification, and suggested reviewer question. The prompt demands exhaustive step-by-step analysis in the customer-visible response. Tests show no quality improvement over a concise rubric-based response, but latency and token use rise substantially. Legal needs defensible evidence, not an internal reasoning transcript. Which change BEST addresses the measured problem while retaining the required justification?

options.text: Remove the cited justification and reviewer question, returning only the risk label so all explanation tokens are eliminated consistently.
options.why: It cuts required output and legal evidence rather than the unnecessary exhaustive reasoning requirement.

options.text: Require two separate exhaustive reasoning drafts and let a smaller model summarize them before returning the same structured risk assessment.
options.why: Extra drafts multiply work without measured quality benefit and retain the unnecessary analysis cost.

options.text: Keep exhaustive visible reasoning but stream it sooner, treating earlier first tokens as proof that the completed-response latency requirement now passes.
options.why: Streaming can improve perceived responsiveness without reducing total generation time or proving completion targets.

options.text: Request the structured risk label, concise evidence-backed justification, and reviewer question; evaluate quality and latency again without requiring exhaustive visible reasoning.
options.why: The output contract meets legal needs while removing unhelpful verbosity demonstrated to add cost and latency.

questions.decision: Optimize the required output contract against evidence; useful justification is distinct from demanding a long customer-visible reasoning trace.

questions.title: A long document is not always a long-context task
questions.stem: A technical assistant answers precise questions about numbered clauses in large manuals. Current requests upload entire manuals, but 92% of questions name a specific clause and its referenced table. A retrieval prototype reliably obtains both, while open-ended comparison questions still need broader context. The team must reduce input cost without losing citation coverage. Which TWO changes BEST exploit this measured query shape while protecting exceptional questions?

options.text: Choose the longest-context model for every query and lower the output token limit to offset the cost of repeatedly sending complete manuals.
options.why: Shorter output does not remove unnecessary input cost and may restrict required answers.

options.text: Keep a separately evaluated broader-context path for comparison questions and retrieval insufficiency, monitoring coverage failures and routing mistakes by query class.
options.why: The minority pattern has different evidence needs and must not silently inherit the narrow-context assumption.

options.text: Summarize each manual once without section identifiers and use semantic similarity to choose a short paragraph for every future comparison.
options.why: Removing identifiers and reference relationships threatens coverage for precise clauses and cross-section comparison.

options.text: Truncate every uploaded manual to its opening pages, relying on the model’s general technical knowledge to fill in later numbered clauses.
options.why: Clause-specific evidence may occur anywhere, and general knowledge cannot replace the required citations.

options.text: Route clause-specific questions through validated section and reference retrieval, supplying the relevant table and provenance rather than the entire manual by default.
options.why: The common query names a known evidence unit; targeted retrieval reduces context while preserving supporting references.

questions.decision: Match context construction to query shape, preserve references, and explicitly evaluate the routing boundary rather than applying a universal truncation rule.

questions.title: Skills without hidden universal context
questions.stem: A platform group maintains eleven specialist operating procedures. Most tasks need only one, and their detailed examples collectively overwhelm the prompt. A short description can identify when each procedure applies, but some tasks require a general safety baseline regardless of specialty. Which design BEST uses progressive disclosure while avoiding the risk that the mandatory baseline disappears when a specialist procedure is not selected?

options.text: Replace specialist procedures with one long generic example, asking Claude to infer each specialist workflow without consulting the approved instructions.
options.why: A generic example discards the approved task-specific guidance rather than disclosing it progressively.

options.text: Keep the universal baseline durable, expose concise specialist descriptions, and load detailed procedures when the task needs them.
options.why: It preserves universal constraints while making optional specialized detail available on demand.

options.text: Load the eleven complete procedures on every turn but ask Claude to ignore examples that do not apply to the current request.
options.why: Ignoring irrelevant text does not recover the consumed context or reduce interference.

options.text: Move all instructions, including the mandatory safety baseline, into a specialist procedure so the initial prompt contains only procedure names.
options.why: The baseline becomes conditional on successful discovery and loading, contrary to its universal requirement.

questions.decision: Progressive disclosure is appropriate for optional detail, while genuinely universal authority must remain reliably available independent of specialty selection.

questions.title: A near-miss extraction example
questions.stem: A document extractor returns a shipment date from invoices. The schema allows a date or null. Examples use invoices where the issue date and shipment date match. In production, it incorrectly returns the issue date when no shipment date exists. The business wants the smallest prompt intervention that targets the error while preserving extraction from genuine shipment fields. Which option is BEST?

options.text: Rename the output field to a more detailed label while retaining the examples where both dates match and omitting missing-field guidance.
options.why: A better name alone leaves the demonstrated ambiguity in every example and no explicit absence behavior.

options.text: Ask for a longer explanation after each selected date, retaining the same examples and accepting any explanation that mentions shipping.
options.why: An explanation can rationalize the same wrong field and does not resolve the missing-evidence contract.

options.text: Add contrasting examples with distinct issue and shipment dates plus missing shipment dates, explicitly requiring null when shipment evidence is absent.
options.why: Contrasts teach the specific distinction and missing-evidence behavior without changing the valid schema.

options.text: Require a date for every invoice and use the issue date as an approved substitute whenever a shipment field cannot be found.
options.why: The substitution changes the business semantics and removes the existing valid null response.

questions.decision: Use discriminating examples that exercise the near-miss and absent-evidence cases; extra wording is useful only when it clarifies the actual distinction.

questions.title: Capability pruning before better selection
questions.stem: An operations assistant resolves inventory discrepancies. Its tool catalog includes twelve inventory read tools and eight purchasing mutation tools inherited from a broader prototype. The approved role is read-only, and selection errors increasingly involve similar tool names. The team plans better tool descriptions but must first reduce unauthorized action exposure. Which intervention BEST satisfies the role boundary while directly simplifying the available capability surface?

options.text: Rename purchasing tools with a warning prefix and include examples showing that inventory discrepancy questions should normally use read tools.
options.why: Naming may reduce confusion but retains unauthorized capabilities and their credentials.

options.text: Keep the purchasing tools but describe them as emergency-only, requiring the assistant to explain any decision to use one.
options.why: Descriptions and explanations leave forbidden write capabilities reachable and do not enforce the read-only role.

options.text: Remove purchasing tools and write credentials, retain inventory reads, then tune remaining descriptions against representative discrepancy requests.
options.why: It removes unnecessary action authority and selection candidates, then addresses remaining usability issues.

options.text: Add a tool-selection classifier that hides purchasing tools from ordinary requests while retaining their write credentials for unusual discrepancies.
options.why: An inferred unusual request is not authority to expand an explicitly read-only role.

questions.decision: Prune capabilities that the role cannot use before optimizing discovery or descriptions of the capabilities that remain.

questions.title: Authentication stops at the wrong boundary
questions.stem: A remote MCP server validates the caller’s signed access token and confirms its audience. It then accepts an account identifier in tool arguments and retrieves that account using a service credential. All users in a company authenticate successfully, but only assigned account managers may view particular accounts. Which TWO controls most directly close the remaining authorization gap without confusing token validity with account-level permission?

options.text: Scope the downstream service access and bind account selection to server-validated authorization context, logging denied cross-account attempts without exposing account contents.
options.why: Defense in depth limits service reach and makes unauthorized attempts observable without leaking data.

options.text: Ask Claude to compare the requested account identifier with the user’s stated job title before deciding whether to invoke the read tool.
options.why: A user-stated title and model judgment are not server-enforced account authorization.

options.text: Extend token expiry so managers do not encounter repeated authentication prompts while navigating between accounts during an active session.
options.why: Longer validity improves convenience but does not evaluate the missing account assignment.

options.text: Accept any company-issued token at the account API because the MCP server already verified its signature and intended audience.
options.why: Company membership and token validity do not confer permission to every protected account.

options.text: Resolve the authenticated principal and evaluate its assignment to the requested account on every protected tool execution before reading account data.
options.why: A valid identity must still be authorized for the specific resource and operation.

questions.decision: Authentication establishes who called; authorization determines whether that caller may perform this operation on this account at execution time.

questions.title: Accuracy at a fixed completion deadline
questions.stem: A knowledge service compares retrieval configurations on a representative workload. The signed service target requires answer support of at least 96% and p95 completed latency no greater than 2.4 seconds. Operational cost is minimized only among passing configurations, and all share the same access controls. Results include reranking and generation. Which configuration should the architect recommend for the controlled release described by the exhibit?

options.text: Recommend Ridge because its greater answer support should offset its slightly slower tail response for most users in practice.
options.why: The contract contains a latency gate; a quality gain does not authorize exceeding it.

options.text: Recommend Valley because it delivers the lowest measured cost and fastest completed responses, with support close to the required threshold.
options.why: Close to the threshold is insufficient when the agreed gate requires at least 96% support.

options.text: Recommend Harbor because it passes both measured service gates and has the lowest cost of the configurations that satisfy those gates.
options.why: Harbor costs less than Summit; Valley fails support and Ridge fails latency.

options.text: Recommend Summit because it has the strongest support among the latency-compliant configurations, regardless of the stated secondary cost objective.
options.why: Both Harbor and Summit pass, so the explicit cost objective favors Harbor.

questions.decision: Treat contractual quality and tail latency as independent gates, then minimize cost using measured end-to-end results rather than isolated stages.

questions.title: A distributed trace with restricted content
questions.stem: A retail assistant spans a gateway, retrieval service, Claude call, and order-status API across three teams. Customers report intermittent slow answers, but each team shows acceptable average latency. Security prohibits raw payment details in telemetry. The incident owner needs to locate slow paths and correlate them with versions and errors. Which THREE observability changes BEST address this problem while respecting the telemetry boundary?

options.text: Log complete prompts, retrieved customer records, and payment payloads in a shared trace so every team can reproduce requests immediately.
options.why: Immediate convenience does not override the explicit prohibition on raw payment data in telemetry.

options.text: Continue reporting team-level averages but page all three teams whenever any customer’s response exceeds an individually chosen latency threshold.
options.why: Uncorrelated averages cannot identify the critical path, and arbitrary alerts do not resolve the measurement gap.

options.text: Redact prohibited fields at collection, retain authorized operational metadata, and assign alert ownership with a documented incident response path.
options.why: It preserves useful diagnostics without violating the content boundary and makes response accountable.

options.text: Propagate a request correlation identifier through stage spans, recording start, duration, dependency outcome, and parent relationships for the full customer operation.
options.why: Correlated spans reveal which dependencies and paths compose the actual slow operation.

options.text: Measure end-to-end and stage tail latency by relevant workload slice, retaining prompt, retrieval, and deployment version identifiers for comparison.
options.why: Tails and versioned slices expose regressions that averages can conceal.

questions.decision: Customer latency is a correlated system property; operational evidence should retain timings and version context while excluding prohibited content.

questions.title: The correct clause at the wrong time
questions.stem: A lease assistant uses structure-aware chunks that preserve headings, tables, and document relationships. Retrieval finds the correct clause number but sometimes uses a renewal amendment when answering questions about an earlier accounting period. Chunks retain effective-date intervals and lease identifiers, and both versions must remain searchable for historical questions. Which indexing and retrieval change BEST targets the remaining defect without deleting valid history?

options.text: Delete superseded clauses from the index so only the latest renewal terms can be retrieved for either current or historical accounting questions.
options.why: Deleting valid historical evidence violates the requirement to answer earlier-period questions.

options.text: Filter or select evidence by the requested lease and effective interval, preserving supersession relationships and citing the version applicable to that period.
options.why: The missing constraint is temporal applicability, not chunk structure; both historical and current versions remain useful.

options.text: Increase chunk overlap around each already-complete clause and table, retaining the existing version-agnostic candidate selection and answer generation behavior.
options.why: More local context does not choose the effective version for the requested period.

options.text: Merge every version of the clause into one generated summary and cite the latest amendment regardless of the accounting period requested.
options.why: A merged latest-version summary can silently apply current terms to a historical question.

questions.decision: Good chunk boundaries do not settle which version applies. Match temporal and entity constraints explicitly while preserving valid historical evidence.

questions.title: Aggregation over a structured relationship
questions.stem: A finance assistant answers how much subsidiaries controlled by Company L spent with Supplier R during the previous quarter. Ownership dates, invoice amounts, currencies, and supplier identifiers reside in structured tables. Policy explanations are stored in a separate document index. Dense retrieval finds convincing invoice excerpts but omits some subsidiaries and double-counts duplicated records. Which TWO changes BEST support accurate, authorized aggregate answers for this query shape?

options.text: Return the computed result with period, relationship assumptions, and traceable record provenance, then use Claude to explain it alongside separately retrieved policy context.
options.why: It preserves computation evidence and keeps explanatory policy retrieval distinct from the authoritative numeric result.

options.text: Increase dense top-k until retrieved invoice excerpts fill the context, then let Claude infer whether the sample includes every subsidiary and invoice.
options.why: A larger similarity sample does not establish relational completeness or reliable duplicate elimination.

options.text: Use an authorized structured query or calculation service to resolve ownership intervals, deduplicate invoice identities, normalize supplied currencies, and calculate the requested quarter total.
options.why: The query requires complete relational filtering and exact aggregation rather than a handful of similar text excerpts.

options.text: Apply a keyword search for Supplier R and use the sum of amounts mentioned in the first matching pages as the authoritative quarter total.
options.why: Keyword matching does not enforce ownership intervals, currency normalization, or unique invoice identity.

options.text: Summarize each subsidiary annual report into one paragraph and add those summaries together, assuming each report uses the same ownership interval and quarter.
options.why: The assumptions ignore ownership dates and accounting periods, so the aggregation can count inapplicable evidence.

questions.decision: Match retrieval to the data operation: entity relationships, time intervals, deduplication, and sums belong in a governed structured computation, with language used for explanation.

questions.title: A stable backend does not need discovery
questions.stem: A nightly billing reconciliation service must call two stable internal endpoints with documented typed contracts. It runs without an interactive assistant, uses a dedicated service identity, and does not need runtime tool discovery. Another team proposes adding an MCP server because it is the preferred interface for their desktop assistants. Which integration choice BEST fits the stated reconciliation service and avoids introducing an unsupported authorization assumption?

options.text: Introduce MCP and reuse desktop users' broad access tokens so the nightly service automatically inherits all existing interactive capabilities.
options.why: Interactive user authority is not an appropriate default service identity and adds unnecessary capability reach.

options.text: Use a shell command that accesses the database with an administrator credential, avoiding API contracts that may reject unusual reconciliation cases.
options.why: Bypassing typed contracts and scoped identity sacrifices controls without satisfying any stated need.

options.text: Convert the two endpoints into an agent-to-agent conversation so independent agents can negotiate how each night’s billing reconciliation should proceed.
options.why: A stable deterministic integration has no demonstrated need for negotiated autonomous coordination.

options.text: Use existing typed APIs with scoped service identity, retries, and monitoring; revisit MCP when a concrete interoperability requirement emerges.
options.why: The workload has stable direct contracts and no current discovery or assistant-client requirement.

questions.decision: Choose protocols for the actual client and contract requirements; a useful assistant protocol is not automatically the best backend service interface.

questions.title: Discovery should preserve essential routing tools
questions.stem: An enterprise assistant can access 460 approved tools, but most requests use two or three. Loading every schema consumes substantial context. Tests of deferred discovery reduce context use but sometimes fail to discover the task-status tool needed to resume a long-running job. The tool is small and needed on every resume path. Which TWO changes BEST preserve the benefit while correcting this demonstrated discovery failure?

options.text: Test discovery recall, schema load cost, selection accuracy, and completed-task latency on new jobs and resume scenarios before releasing the revised configuration.
options.why: The evaluation covers both the original efficiency goal and the newly exposed resume failure.

options.text: Keep the small essential task-status interface directly available, while deferring the large specialized catalog behind well-described discovery entries.
options.why: Universal resume functionality need not depend on discovery; specialized schemas retain their context savings.

options.text: Keep all tools deferred and lengthen the general system prompt with every possible wording users might use when asking about job progress.
options.why: Exhaustive phrasing increases context and still makes essential status access depend on successful discovery.

options.text: Return every specialized schema whenever a resume request occurs so the status tool is guaranteed to appear among all available capabilities.
options.why: It restores the large context burden instead of isolating the small universally needed interface.

options.text: Remove the task-status tool from the catalog and ask Claude to infer completion from its saved description of the previous job.
options.why: A saved narrative is not an authoritative current status source for an external long-running operation.

questions.decision: Deferral is selective: keep small essential interfaces immediate, discover optional detail, and evaluate the resume path rather than only new-task success.

questions.title: A token forwarded to the wrong resource
questions.stem: A remote MCP server receives an access token intended for itself. Its downstream document API expects a token issued for that separate resource. A developer forwards the original token, arguing that both services trust the same identity provider. Security testing shows inconsistent acceptance across environments. Which repair BEST respects resource-specific authorization rather than relying on coincidental downstream token acceptance?

options.text: Remove audience validation at the MCP server because the identity provider’s signature proves the token was issued by a trusted organization.
options.why: Issuer trust alone does not show that the token is intended for the receiving resource.

options.text: Configure the document API to accept tokens for either resource so the existing forwarded token works consistently across deployment environments.
options.why: Broadening accepted audiences to accommodate passthrough weakens resource separation rather than establishing proper delegation.

options.text: Validate the MCP token audience, establish separate downstream authorization, and enforce current document permissions at the downstream boundary.
options.why: Resource audience and downstream delegation are distinct; each boundary requires appropriate authorization.

options.text: Keep token forwarding but ask users to confirm document access once per session, treating the confirmation as sufficient downstream resource authorization.
options.why: User confirmation does not change token audience or prove document authorization at the downstream API.

questions.decision: A token is not a universal identity pass. Validate resource intent and establish appropriate downstream authority instead of passing through incompatible credentials.

questions.title: Parallel reads without speculative writes
questions.stem: A procurement assistant retrieves a supplier profile and shipment history before drafting a response. Each read is independent, authorized, and idempotent. Placing an order depends on both results and an approved draft; it must never occur speculatively. Traces show the reads dominate response time. Which TWO integration changes BEST reduce the critical path while preserving the stated dependency and approval requirements?

options.text: Parallelize drafting and approval by approving a generic template before the actual supplier and shipment details return to the assistant.
options.why: Generic approval does not bind the eventual evidence-dependent transaction that will execute.

options.text: Remove one read permanently because its latency appears similar to the other read, treating matching timing as evidence that it is redundant.
options.why: Equal latency says nothing about whether the two sources provide interchangeable evidence.

options.text: Keep order placement behind the completed validation and approval boundary, preserving operation identity and uncertain-outcome handling for any subsequent execution.
options.why: The consequential effect remains dependent on the required results and approved intent.

options.text: Execute the independent authorized reads concurrently, then join their results before drafting and validating the recommendation against both evidence sets.
options.why: Parallel independent reads remove unnecessary sequential delay without bypassing result dependencies.

options.text: Begin order placement concurrently with the reads and cancel it later if the supplier profile or shipment history suggests a problem.
options.why: Cancellation may occur after an irreversible external effect and violates the no-speculation requirement.

questions.decision: Parallelize tasks whose inputs and effects permit it; do not turn dependent or consequential work into speculative execution merely to shorten latency.

questions.title: Revocation in a derived index
questions.stem: A policy assistant retrieves indexed project documents. When a project is closed, its source-system access list changes immediately, but the vector index refreshes nightly. Recently removed staff can still retrieve old project chunks during that interval. The business requires access revocation to take effect before the next query, independent of content refresh timing. Which integration design BEST satisfies that requirement?

options.text: Increase nightly indexing frequency to every hour and document that the index usually catches access-list changes within the improved interval.
options.why: Any positive interval can still violate the requirement that revocation precede the next query.

options.text: Encrypt the vector index at rest and keep its existing retrieval authorization because the data is protected while no query is running.
options.why: At-rest encryption does not stop an unauthorized query from receiving decrypted project chunks.

options.text: Retain the index behavior but add a prompt asking Claude not to mention project information when the user says they have changed roles.
options.why: User disclosure and prompt obedience are not an enforced check against the current access list.

options.text: Evaluate current project authorization at query time before exposing candidates, and propagate document deletions and version changes through the index lifecycle separately.
options.why: Current authorization blocks stale-index disclosure without assuming immediate content refresh.

questions.decision: Content freshness and authorization freshness are different contracts. A stale content index must not become the authority for current resource access.

questions.title: The monitoring cardinality trap
questions.stem: A large assistant deployment labels every metric with complete user text, document identifier, request identifier, and model version. Monitoring costs spike, dashboards time out, and privacy reviewers object to sensitive text in labels. Incident responders still need aggregate service trends and the ability to investigate a permitted individual request. Which design BEST preserves both needs with an appropriate separation of metric and trace responsibilities?

options.text: Hash complete user text into a metric label and keep the remaining identifiers, assuming hashing alone solves cost and privacy concerns.
options.why: Distinct hashes retain high cardinality, and hashing is not an automatic privacy or retention justification.

options.text: Keep aggregate metrics on bounded operational dimensions, place permitted request-level identifiers in correlated access-controlled traces, and exclude sensitive text at collection.
options.why: It controls metric cardinality while retaining authorized request investigation and minimizing sensitive data.

options.text: Retain every label but sample dashboards once daily so the monitoring backend stores fewer displayed points and sensitive values appear less often.
options.why: Dashboard sampling does not remove the underlying high-cardinality series or prohibited text collection.

options.text: Remove all identifiers from metrics and traces, retaining only deployment-wide averages to eliminate every chance of sensitive request correlation.
options.why: It discards the required ability to investigate an individual permitted request and hides tail behavior.

questions.decision: Use bounded metric labels for trends and controlled traces for request detail; collection minimization must precede storage rather than rely on dashboard presentation.

questions.title: The success metric rewards abandonment
questions.stem: A utilities assistant is judged by the percentage of conversations closed without human transfer. The latest version improves that metric, but disputed bills rise because customers give up after unsupported explanations. The utility needs accurate resolution, with escalation available for cases the assistant cannot safely resolve. Which evaluation change BEST distinguishes real improvement from the metric manipulation observed in production without penalizing appropriate human transfers?

options.text: Grade final-message groundedness, response latency, and model cost, treating grounded explanations as successful resolution without linking them to subsequent billing disputes.
options.why: Grounded communication can still fail to resolve the issue; the downstream resolution and dispute outcome remains unmeasured.

options.text: Measure independently verified resolution and subsequent disputes alongside groundedness, safe escalation, latency, and total handling cost, with explicit acceptance thresholds.
options.why: It evaluates actual service success and recognizes appropriate escalation rather than treating every closure as success.

options.text: Track first-contact resolution as closure without transfer, auditing only transferred cases for correctness and comparing their handling time and direct model costs.
options.why: Closed and abandoned cases remain unaudited, preserving the exact false-success channel and incomplete cost boundary.

options.text: Survey users who complete the conversation and measure their satisfaction, excluding abandoned conversations because no final resolution rating can be reliably collected.
options.why: Excluding abandonment removes the cases that reveal the demonstrated harm and biases the outcome estimate.

questions.decision: A proxy that rewards premature closure needs outcome-based correction. Appropriate escalation can be a successful safety behavior rather than an evaluation failure.

questions.title: An evaluation set with repeated evidence
questions.stem: A compliance assistant’s dataset contains many near-duplicate questions generated from the same policy paragraphs. Random splitting puts paraphrases of each paragraph into both development and test sets. Scores are high, but new policy families fail. The team needs credible evidence of generalization and critical-case performance before the next release. Which TWO dataset changes BEST address this weakness without discarding useful known-case regression coverage?

options.text: Move all low-scoring new-family cases into the development split and report only the remaining stable test questions during release review.
options.why: Removing hard cases from evaluation hides the exact deployment risk that needs measurement.

options.text: Generate more paraphrases of existing questions and retain the same random split, assuming greater dataset size will dilute any source overlap.
options.why: More correlated paraphrases increase volume without correcting the leakage boundary.

options.text: Maintain separate known-case regression and new-family challenge slices, including critical exceptions and independently reviewed expected behavior with provenance.
options.why: Distinct slices retain regression protection while measuring new-family and risk-sensitive capability.

options.text: Partition held-out testing by source family or policy group, preventing near-duplicate evidence and paraphrases from crossing the development-test boundary.
options.why: Grouping prevents the leakage that makes random question-level splitting overstate generalization.

options.text: Use the model’s answer to each paraphrase as its expected label, avoiding the cost of reviewing policy-family exceptions with subject experts.
options.why: Self-labeling cannot establish correctness and can preserve the model’s systematic exception errors.

questions.decision: Generalization is about unseen evidence groups, not just unseen wording. Keep regression and challenge evidence separate and preserve independently grounded labels.

questions.title: Conversation turns contaminate the experiment
questions.stem: A support team A/B tests two prompts by randomly assigning each message independently. Long conversations therefore receive both prompts, and the reported effect favors the new prompt when it appears late in a conversation that the original prompt has already clarified. The decision concerns complete customer-case outcomes, not isolated message ratings. Which redesign BEST makes the experiment relevant and avoids the demonstrated treatment contamination?

options.text: Assign complete conversations consistently to one version and compare case outcomes using prespecified gates and conversation-level analysis.
options.why: Stable conversation assignment aligns treatment with the outcome and prevents versions from sharing one conversation’s causal history.

options.text: Continue message-level randomization but use a larger sample so any advantage from appearing late in a conversation becomes statistically insignificant.
options.why: Larger samples do not remove systematic treatment contamination or misaligned outcome units.

options.text: Ask an LLM judge to guess which version caused the case outcome from the blended transcript, using its confidence as experiment significance.
options.why: A judge’s causal guess cannot repair the contaminated assignment design.

options.text: Give the new prompt only the final message in every conversation and compare final-message ratings with the original prompt’s earlier ratings.
options.why: Different conversation stages remain confounded and do not identify the effect on complete case outcomes.

questions.decision: Choose the experimental unit that matches the decision and preserves a consistent treatment history; more observations do not fix an invalid assignment unit.

questions.title: Three kinds of evidence for an agent
questions.stem: A travel assistant reports that reservations were changed successfully, but database checks reveal some unchanged bookings. Other outputs are technically correct yet confusing to travelers. The release suite currently grades only the final message using a general LLM judge. Which TWO additions BEST improve the suite while separating externally verifiable success from judgment about the quality of user-facing communication in this workflow?

options.text: Use a task-specific communication rubric calibrated against human reviews, testing clarity and disclosure separately from the state-based success checks.
options.why: Human-calibrated judgment evaluates subjective communication without replacing objective outcome verification.

options.text: Use two more general judges on the final message and replace database checks whenever the judges agree that the change sounds plausible.
options.why: Consensus about the narrative is still not evidence of actual booking state.

options.text: Grade the number of tool calls, accepting every attempt with at least one booking tool invocation as a completed successful change.
options.why: Invocation may fail or change the wrong state; activity count is not outcome verification.

options.text: Add deterministic checks against isolated booking state and allowed tool effects, verifying the requested change occurred without unauthorized alterations.
options.why: External state proves task outcome more directly than a convincing final message.

options.text: Require the assistant to restate the reservation identifier twice in its final message, counting matching strings as proof that the booking changed.
options.why: The same identifier can appear even when no external state change occurred.

questions.decision: Verify observable outcomes with deterministic state evidence and evaluate subjective communication with calibrated rubrics; neither should stand in for the other.

questions.title: A retrieval failure that looks like reasoning
questions.stem: A financial-research assistant becomes wrong on newly updated filings after a release. The model and prompt remain unchanged. Investigation can replay the same questions with either the old index, new index, or verified relevant excerpts. The exhibit reports grounded correctness on the same cases; old filings remain stable. Which first investigation BEST follows the supplied evidence before changing the model or rewriting the system prompt?

options.text: Roll back the model version even though the release changed only the index, prioritizing the most visible AI component in the incident.
options.why: The unchanged model is not the demonstrated changed dependency, and replay evidence points to the index.

options.text: Inspect new-index ingestion, chunk construction, version filtering, and retrieval for updated filings, using verified excerpts as a control for downstream answer generation.
options.why: Restored performance with verified excerpts isolates the changed evidence pipeline as the first likely failure layer.

options.text: Increase the model’s reasoning budget for every request because updated filings require more advanced analysis than the existing filings in the benchmark.
options.why: The verified-excerpt control shows the unchanged model can answer those cases well with correct evidence.

options.text: Rewrite the prompt to demand stronger confidence because new-index answers may be overly cautious about financial evidence from recent documents.
options.why: Confidence wording does not explain the observed index-dependent correctness collapse.

questions.decision: Use controlled replay to localize the failure. A generator that recovers with verified evidence does not justify model replacement as the first intervention.

questions.title: A feedback event is not a training label
questions.stem: A production assistant collects thumbs-down events. Some indicate factual errors, others object to an unpopular but correct policy, and a few are spam. A developer proposes feeding every negative case directly into prompt examples each night. The service owner wants responsive improvements without unstable behavior or silent policy reversal. Which TWO steps BEST turn this feedback stream into useful evaluation and controlled iteration?

options.text: Test proposed changes against affected and unaffected slices, require the relevant release gates, and deploy versioned changes with monitoring and rollback ownership.
options.why: Controlled release prevents local fixes from silently degrading other behavior and preserves accountability.

options.text: Triage feedback into error types with source and version context, confirming labels and policy intent before adding representative cases to evaluation.
options.why: The event is ambiguous; classification and verification distinguish correctness problems from dissatisfaction or abuse.

options.text: Optimize the nightly prompt only for fewer negative events, allowing the assistant to soften mandatory restrictions whenever customers react unfavorably.
options.why: Fewer complaints can result from violating policy, so the metric cannot substitute for correctness and safety gates.

options.text: Convert every negative event into an opposite-answer example, assuming user rejection implies the earlier policy interpretation was substantively wrong.
options.why: Negative feedback does not establish that the answer or policy was incorrect.

options.text: Hide disputed cases from the evaluation dashboard until the next policy review, so engineers can improve response style without distracting release owners.
options.why: It conceals potentially material errors rather than collecting and resolving the evidence.

questions.decision: Feedback initiates investigation; it is not self-validating supervision. Curate evidence, test changes across slices, and close the loop through controlled releases.

questions.title: Choose a cache lifetime for bursty reuse
questions.stem: Thirty requests share one eligible stable prefix, arriving in three ten-request bursts at minutes zero, twenty, and forty; each burst completes within one minute. Supplied fictional prefix charges are $0.025 per five-minute write, $0.040 per one-hour write, and $0.002 per read under either lifetime. No eviction or prefix changes occur. Dynamic and output costs are identical. Which configuration minimizes total prefix charges for this workload?

options.text: Use the one-hour cache: three writes and twenty-seven reads cost $0.174 because each new burst requires a separate write regardless of lifetime.
options.why: The prefix is still cached at minutes twenty and forty under the one-hour lifetime, so those are reads.

options.text: Use the five-minute cache: one write and twenty-nine reads cost $0.083 because all requests share the same prefix text.
options.why: Identical text does not prevent expiration across gaps longer than five minutes.

options.text: Use the one-hour cache: one write and twenty-nine reads cost $0.098, compared with $0.129 for three five-minute writes and twenty-seven reads.
options.why: The higher one-hour write cost is offset by retaining the prefix across both twenty-minute gaps.

options.text: Use the five-minute cache: its lower write price makes three writes and twenty-seven reads cost $0.075, below the one-hour alternative.
options.why: It counts the three writes but omits the twenty-seven charged reads.

questions.decision: Compare lifetime choices against the actual reuse gaps and charged categories. One-hour: .040+29×.002=.098; five-minute: 3×.025+27×.002=.129.

rows: Each burst finishes within one minute

questions.title: A gain with an unacceptable subgroup
questions.stem: A document-assistance release candidate raises aggregate correctness from 94% to 96% on a balanced test set. It also increases unsupported critical claims for one regulated document class. The release agreement requires no critical-claim regression in any regulated class; the product owner says the global gain should compensate. Which TWO actions BEST honor the agreed evidence standard while still allowing the promising candidate to be improved?

options.text: Release the candidate globally but add a general disclaimer explaining that AI-generated document summaries can sometimes include unsupported claims.
options.why: A disclaimer does not satisfy the stipulated no-regression requirement for regulated classes.

options.text: Remove the failing document class from monitoring because its low production volume would otherwise make the dashboard statistically noisy.
options.why: Excluding the slice conceals the known material risk instead of measuring or repairing it.

options.text: Investigate and repair the failing class, then retest it and protected regression slices under the same versioned acceptance criteria.
options.why: It preserves the improvement opportunity while requiring evidence that the actual release obligation is met.

options.text: Block broad release under the current agreement and present the class-specific critical regression alongside the aggregate gain to the accountable release owner.
options.why: The independent critical-class gate is violated and cannot be averaged away.

options.text: Reweight the test set toward high-volume unregulated documents until the overall unsupported-claim rate falls below its earlier aggregate level.
options.why: Changing weights hides an independent regulated-class failure and alters the agreed standard after observing results.

questions.decision: An independent critical gate is not a weighted preference. Preserve promising improvements through targeted repair and evidence, not metric redefinition.

questions.title: A faster first token misses the actual goal
questions.stem: A drafting assistant must finish usable answers within six seconds at p95. Streaming now makes the first token arrive after one second, but completed drafts still take nine seconds. Traces show excessive repetitive output, while retrieval and tool reads are already fast. The business permits shorter drafts if required facts and citations remain. Which optimization hypothesis BEST follows the demonstrated bottleneck and the actual service target?

options.text: Declare the streaming change successful because users now see an initial token well before the six-second deadline in almost every case.
options.why: First-token latency does not establish the explicitly required completed-answer latency.

options.text: Reduce redundant generated text through a concise output contract, then measure completed-answer latency, required coverage, and quality on representative long-output cases.
options.why: The dominant generation workload and completion metric are directly targeted while preserving required content.

options.text: Add a retrieval reranker to every request because better evidence ranking generally improves perceived answer quality and user trust.
options.why: Retrieval is already fast, and additional reranking does not target repetitive output or the completion bottleneck.

options.text: Increase the maximum output allowance so the assistant never truncates, expecting the larger available budget to accelerate production of the required draft.
options.why: An increased allowance does not shorten generation and may enable still more redundant text.

questions.decision: Optimize the critical path and the latency metric actually promised. Streaming responsiveness and completed usable output are different outcomes.

questions.title: Two versions changed together
questions.stem: A team deploys a new prompt and a new retrieval index in the same release. Correctness falls on one product family while latency remains stable. Logs retain both version identifiers, and a safe replay environment can combine either prompt with either index on a fixed set of labeled cases. Which diagnostic plan BEST distinguishes causes before investing in a model upgrade or wider rollout?

options.text: Replay all four prompt-index combinations on the affected and control slices, inspect retrieved evidence, and compare errors against the fixed labels.
options.why: A controlled factorial replay separates prompt, index, and interaction effects while checking the relevant slice.

options.text: Upgrade the model first and retest only the new prompt with the new index, since stronger reasoning can compensate for either changed component.
options.why: Compensation obscures the causal fault and adds another variable before identifying the regression.

options.text: Ask the model to explain which release component caused each incorrect answer, accepting the most frequent explanation as the root cause.
options.why: Self-explanations are not controlled evidence of which changed component introduced the error.

options.text: Compare average production latency before and after deployment, treating stable timing as evidence that the retrieval index is not responsible.
options.why: Correctness defects can occur with unchanged latency; timing does not exonerate retrieval quality.

questions.decision: Use available versioned controls to isolate changes and their interaction; stable latency or fluent causal explanations do not identify correctness causes.

questions.title: A retrieved instruction crosses an action boundary
questions.stem: A contract assistant reads supplier PDFs and can draft internal review tasks. A malicious PDF tells it to attach confidential pricing to an external address. The assistant currently has a general email tool for unrelated workflows, though this role never requires external messages. Security wants the most direct architectural reduction of the demonstrated risk before adding detection heuristics. Which change BEST addresses the role’s actual authority?

options.text: Keep external email but ask the model to identify malicious phrasing in each PDF before deciding whether sending information is appropriate.
