options.why: A classifier may help detect attacks but leaves unnecessary external capability reachable.

options.text: Send a warning email to security after every external message so investigators can quickly identify supplier documents responsible for disclosures.
options.why: Post-disclosure detection is weaker than removing a capability the role does not need.

options.text: Remove external-send authority, treat PDF instructions as untrusted content, and test exfiltration attempts against the remaining authorized interfaces.
options.why: It removes unnecessary external authority and reinforces the trust boundary that the PDF attempted to cross.

options.text: Allow external email only when the PDF contains an explicit recipient and a sufficiently detailed justification that the model can cite.
options.why: Untrusted source text cannot authorize disclosure merely by supplying a plausible rationale and recipient.

questions.decision: Remove unnecessary action authority first, then layer content defenses and evaluations; untrusted documents cannot create permission to disclose information.

questions.title: An approval queue that cannot be staffed
questions.stem: A clinical-document assistant sends uncertain summaries to human reviewers before any clinical use. At peak load the review queue exceeds staffing capacity, and a proposed timeout would publish unreviewed summaries after fifteen minutes. The organization’s approved policy requires review for those uncertain cases. Which TWO design changes BEST preserve that policy while exposing the operational capacity problem rather than disguising it as automation?

options.text: Publish timed-out summaries with a disclaimer and mark them reviewed later if a clinician eventually confirms that the content was acceptable.
options.why: A later review does not satisfy a required pre-use review, and a disclaimer changes no authority.

options.text: Raise the model’s confidence threshold until the review queue fits current staffing, using self-reported confidence without calibration as the routing signal.
options.why: Uncalibrated confidence cannot justify shrinking the set of cases requiring review.

options.text: Measure arrival rates, reviewer service time, and queue-age tails; agree staffing, scope, or service-target changes with the responsible clinical owner.
options.why: Capacity evidence supports an explicit operational decision instead of weakening the safety contract.

options.text: Treat summaries as implicitly approved when their assigned reviewer is online, assuming active availability means the reviewer could have intervened.
options.why: Availability is not an affirmative review of the particular summary before use.

options.text: Keep uncertain outputs withheld when approval times out, expose their pending status, and route capacity exceptions through an approved operational fallback.
options.why: A timeout cannot silently convert a required review into permission to publish.

questions.decision: Human oversight is an operational system with capacity and timeout behavior. When review is required, insufficient staffing must trigger an explicit fallback, not implicit approval.

questions.title: Encryption does not settle the cloud obligation
questions.stem: A hospital plans to send encrypted patient-document archives to a cloud service that stores them without holding the decryption key. Counsel confirms the archives remain ePHI and that the cloud operator is acting on the hospital’s behalf. The vendor argues no BAA is needed because employees cannot view the documents. Which response BEST follows the stated role and the relevant cloud-computing guidance?

options.text: Require the appropriate BAA and documented risk analysis and responsibilities before proceeding; lack of the decryption key does not alone remove business-associate obligations.
options.why: HHS explicitly treats no-view storage of ePHI on another party’s behalf as business-associate activity.

options.text: Accept the no-view arrangement as outside HIPAA because technical inability to read an archive means the operator cannot maintain protected health information.
options.why: Maintaining encrypted ePHI still falls within the stated business-associate relationship under HHS guidance.

options.text: Proceed under an ordinary availability SLA alone, because encryption addresses confidentiality and the hospital remains responsible for every other regulatory duty.
options.why: An SLA and encryption do not replace the applicable BAA or the provider’s own relevant obligations.

options.text: Require the vendor to hold a decryption key so it can audit clinical content, treating that access as the missing condition for a valid BAA.
options.why: Additional key access is not a prerequisite for business-associate status and may unnecessarily increase exposure.

questions.decision: Classify the service’s role and data first. No-view encryption affects controls but does not by itself erase stipulated HIPAA business-associate duties.

questions.title: Approval for the operation that executes
questions.stem: A finance assistant prepares supplier-payment proposals. A controller approves a displayed amount, bank account, and invoice identifier. The execution tool then rereads supplier details, which can change before payment. Existing logs record the controller’s name but do not bind approval to a particular proposal version. Which THREE controls BEST preserve meaningful human authorization and safe execution under this time-of-check/time-of-use risk?

options.text: Persist a unique payment operation identifier and reconcile uncertain execution outcomes before retrying, retaining the approval and result in an audit record.
options.why: Idempotency and reconciliation prevent duplicate payments while preserving accountable approved intent.

options.text: Validate current authority and the approved field binding at execution, rejecting stale or inconsistent proposals before any payment is committed.
options.why: Execution-time validation closes the gap between displayed approval and the later external effect.

options.text: Bind approval to the payment’s material fields and proposal version, requiring renewed approval when amount, beneficiary account, or invoice identity changes.
options.why: Approval must apply to the operation that actually executes, not a vaguely related earlier proposal.

options.text: Treat the controller’s authenticated session as approval for all supplier payments prepared during that session, including subsequent beneficiary changes.
options.why: Session identity is broader than an affirmative approval for the changed material transaction.

options.text: Permit changed supplier details when Claude explains why the new account appears legitimate, recording that explanation beside the original controller approval.
options.why: A model explanation cannot expand the controller’s approval to different material payment details.

questions.decision: Human authorization is specific to consequential intent. Bind it to material execution fields and preserve a durable identity through uncertain transport outcomes.

questions.title: Equal overall outcomes hide unequal errors
questions.stem: A hiring-assistance tool recommends which applications need additional human review. No candidate is rejected automatically. Aggregate referral rates are similar across two groups, but the exhibit shows unequal misses among applications that independent reviewers say require review. The agreed safety objective concerns missed necessary reviews, not referral-rate parity. What is the BEST response before broadening this use of the tool?

options.text: Report only the combined missed-review rate because subgroup estimates can be contentious and would slow the planned organizational rollout.
options.why: The pooled metric conceals the known disparity in the agreed harm-relevant measure.

options.text: Force identical referral counts by removing referrals from the higher-referral group until both totals match, without investigating which cases need review.
options.why: Equalizing counts can worsen safety and ignores the independently labeled need for review.

options.text: Investigate missed-review disparity, validate labels and relevant intersections, then reassess each group against the agreed safety objective.
options.why: The stipulated objective concerns false negatives; similar referral rates do not establish that objective or fairness.

options.text: Approve expansion because the two groups receive nearly equal referral rates and all consequential hiring decisions still involve a human reviewer.
options.why: The tool may omit needed review for one group; downstream humans do not necessarily see the missed cases.

questions.decision: Fairness evidence must match the decision’s harm and deployment pathway; parity in one aggregate statistic does not prove equitable error behavior.

questions.title: A scoped erasure request in derived data
questions.stem: A retailer receives an erasure request. Counsel validates the request and defines an approved scope covering identifiable source records, derived retrieval chunks, and application caches; specific legally retained audit records are exempt under a documented retention rule. Engineering can identify the affected copies by lineage. Which TWO actions BEST implement the determined obligation without assuming that deleting the source alone controls every derived artifact?

options.text: Erase the exempt audit records immediately along with every application record, ignoring counsel’s documented exception to simplify the implementation procedure.
options.why: The implementation should honor the legally determined scope, including the stated exception rather than inventing a broader rule.

options.text: Delete or otherwise render inaccessible the in-scope identifiable source and derived copies through a traceable lineage-based workflow, validating completion at each storage boundary.
options.why: The determined scope expressly includes derived chunks and caches, so each must be addressed and checked.

options.text: Retain every derived chunk because embeddings and summaries are automatically anonymous once their original source identifier has been removed.
options.why: Derived text can remain identifiable; removing a direct identifier does not automatically establish anonymization.

options.text: Delete the source record and wait for normal cache expiry and future index refreshes, treating those eventual processes as complete erasure evidence.
options.why: The known derived copies remain accessible and no verified completion of the stipulated obligation exists.

options.text: Apply the documented exemption only to the specified audit records, restricting their permitted use and recording the legally approved basis and retention behavior.
options.why: The explicit exemption is narrow; it does not automatically preserve all operational copies.

questions.decision: Implement the obligation counsel actually determined, including lineage, derived copies, verification, and narrow exceptions; source deletion alone is not evidence of completion.

questions.title: Inherited cloud evidence has a boundary
questions.stem: A federal agency plans an assistant on a cloud service with applicable FedRAMP evidence. The application adds its own document store, user authorization, connector configuration, and incident procedures. A sponsor says the provider’s status means no application-specific security work remains. The agency security team must decide what evidence is still required for this actual deployment. Which response BEST distinguishes inherited assurance from customer-operated responsibilities?

options.text: Replace the security assessment with an assistant-generated compliance statement that lists FedRAMP and the application’s selected encryption algorithms.
options.why: A generated statement is not verified evidence or the agency’s accountable authorization decision.

options.text: Treat the provider’s status as approval of every application using its infrastructure, provided all API calls use encryption in transit.
options.why: Encryption and provider evidence do not establish authorization or control effectiveness for the added application.

options.text: Reuse applicable provider evidence while assessing the actual system boundary, integrations, customer controls, and agency-required authorization and risk-acceptance decisions.
options.why: Provider evidence can reduce duplicated assessment without automatically covering the new application’s controls and boundaries.

options.text: Repeat every provider control assessment from scratch and discard inherited evidence because the application has any customer-managed component.
options.why: It ignores legitimate evidence reuse and imposes unnecessary duplication without addressing the actual boundary efficiently.

questions.decision: Reuse assurance within its demonstrated scope and assess the controls that the customer actually operates; provider status does not automatically authorize the whole application.

questions.title: A screenshot preview is not a sandbox
questions.stem: A design assistant renders user-supplied HTML for preview. Some generated previews contain scripts that attempt network calls or read local files. The assistant itself has no approved reason to expose workstation secrets, and content filtering misses obfuscated code. The team needs controls that remain meaningful if the model produces unsafe HTML. Which TWO choices BEST address the execution boundary rather than relying entirely on generation behavior?

options.text: Add a stronger system instruction asking Claude never to generate unsafe scripts and then render all accepted HTML with ordinary workstation privileges.
options.why: Prompt guidance cannot enforce runtime isolation when unsafe content slips through.

options.text: Render previews in an isolated environment with restricted filesystem access and network egress appropriate to the approved preview purpose.
options.why: Isolation limits what generated content can access even when generation or detection fails.

options.text: Rely on a static denylist of suspicious words and grant full local filesystem access whenever the generated file contains none of them.
options.why: Obfuscation already defeats filtering; absence of denylisted words does not establish safe execution.

options.text: Validate preview artifacts and test adversarial payloads, logging blocked actions without exposing secrets and assigning ownership for containment failures.
options.why: Layered validation and observed failure tests check the actual enforcement boundary.

options.text: Allow unrestricted preview networking because browser rendering requires it, using a generated explanation to justify any outbound request afterward.
options.why: The approved purpose does not require unrestricted egress, and later justification cannot prevent disclosure.

questions.decision: Treat generated executable content as untrusted at the runtime boundary. Constrain its reachable effects and test enforcement rather than assuming perfect generation.

questions.title: An explanation that users can challenge
questions.stem: A benefits assistant helps caseworkers summarize eligibility evidence but does not make final eligibility decisions. Applicants sometimes cannot tell whether an adverse conclusion came from policy, missing records, or an extraction error. The organization requires a practical review route and understandable explanation of relevant evidence. Which design BEST supports transparency and contestability without suggesting that the model’s fluent explanation proves the conclusion is correct?

options.text: Show the caseworker the evidence-linked recommendation, missing information and limitations, identify the accountable decision owner, and provide an applicant correction and review route.
options.why: It distinguishes evidence, uncertainty, and authority while creating a meaningful way to challenge errors.

options.text: Display a numerical confidence score as the entire explanation, assuming a high score gives applicants sufficient information to assess an adverse recommendation.
options.why: A number does not explain the evidence, policy basis, or available correction process.

options.text: Show the applicant a detailed model-generated rationale and remove the caseworker’s identity so the system appears consistent across departments.
options.why: Fluent rationale is not verified correctness, and removing accountable ownership weakens contestability.

options.text: Provide only the final eligibility outcome to avoid overwhelming applicants with technical details, leaving corrections to the normal annual policy-review process.
options.why: It withholds the required relevant explanation and delays practical correction of individual errors.

questions.decision: Transparency should expose evidence, limitations, and accountable review. A convincing generated narrative is not a substitute for verified reasoning and a correction path.

questions.title: Discovery before a product promise
questions.stem: A logistics executive asks for an autonomous exception agent by the end of the quarter. Interviews reveal different meanings of exception, conflicting authority to reroute shipments, and no baseline for current resolution time. A polished demo already exists, and the sales team wants to promise a percentage reduction. Which architect action BEST fits the current lifecycle need before committing an architecture and business improvement target?

options.text: Observe representative exception workflows with operations and risk owners, establish baseline outcomes, and agree decision authority, scope, and measurable acceptance criteria.
options.why: The unresolved problem and authority boundaries must be clarified before defensible design and outcome commitments.

options.text: Document the demo’s components and assign operations an on-call rota so the existing agent can be handed over within the requested quarter.
options.why: Operational handoff is premature while basic scope, authority, and success criteria remain unresolved.

options.text: Commit to the requested autonomous agent and estimate time savings from the demonstration’s fastest completed exception to maintain executive confidence.
options.why: A fastest demo case is not a representative baseline and does not resolve conflicting authority.

options.text: Choose the most capable model and defer exception definitions until users provide feedback after the first broad production deployment.
options.why: Model capability does not settle requirements, and broad deployment exposes unresolved decision authority.

questions.decision: The current work is structured discovery. A demo can test feasibility but cannot establish the agreed problem, authority, or business baseline.

questions.title: Competing stakeholders need explicit constraints
questions.stem: A legal team wants every document retained for audit, privacy wants minimal retention, and operations needs enough evidence to investigate incorrect summaries. The applicable obligations have not yet been interpreted for this use case. An architect is asked to choose a storage design today. Which TWO actions BEST make the trade-off reviewable without pretending the architecture itself can resolve an unmade legal or business decision?

options.text: Implement privacy’s preferred minimum-retention design immediately, leaving legal audit exceptions and operations evidence requirements to be added after the first production release.
options.why: It commits the design before resolving known conflicting obligations and can lose evidence that later cannot be recovered.

options.text: Bring the accountable legal, privacy, and operations owners together to determine applicable purposes, data classes, retention obligations, and permitted diagnostic uses.
options.why: The architecture needs an authorized interpretation of conflicting requirements before choosing retention behavior.

options.text: Present feasible designs with their evidence, exposure, investigation, and deletion trade-offs, recording the chosen obligations and resulting control responsibilities.
options.why: Concrete alternatives let owners make an informed decision that engineers can implement and verify.

options.text: Adopt a uniform ninety-day retention schedule for all source and derived data, using restricted access while stakeholders finish determining the actual applicable obligations.
options.why: A fixed schedule precedes the required obligation determination and can conflict with different purposes or data classes.

options.text: Ask legal to set one retention period from the cloud contract alone, treating derived indexes, diagnostic exports, and investigation uses as implementation details.
options.why: The actual purposes, copies, and operational uses are material to the unresolved obligations, not irrelevant implementation details.

questions.decision: Surface the unresolved authority decision and present implementable options; architecture translates approved obligations rather than inventing them.

questions.title: Trade-offs for an executive decision
questions.stem: A service sponsor must choose between two measured assistant configurations. One meets the current SLA with lower operating cost; the other improves rare complex cases but exceeds the approved budget. Security gates pass for both. The sponsor can authorize a budget change but has not yet done so. Which communication BEST supports an accountable decision without hiding the difficult-case limitation or treating engineering preference as business authority?

options.text: Describe the higher-quality option as technically superior and omit its budget overrun until implementation is underway to avoid confusing the sponsor.
options.why: Withholding a material constraint prevents informed authorization and creates a commitment outside the approved budget.

options.text: Deploy the costly option to complex cases immediately, assuming a sponsor who requested quality improvement implicitly approved any resulting budget increase.
options.why: The sponsor has not authorized the budget change; a quality preference is not unrestricted expenditure authority.

options.text: Present measured outcomes, difficult-case limits, and total costs; recommend the feasible baseline and identify the authorization needed for expansion.
options.why: It makes the recommendation and residual limitation explicit while reserving budget authority for the sponsor.

options.text: Report only cost per token for both models because the sponsor primarily needs a simple comparison rather than operational scenario details.
options.why: Token price omits system outcomes, workload, and the important rare-case trade-off.

questions.decision: Translate technical measurements into the business decision, including feasibility and residual limitations; make required authority visible rather than assuming it.

questions.title: Feedback does not quietly expand the SLA
questions.stem: A pilot assistant supports weekday internal questions with a four-hour human escalation path. Users start relying on it for urgent weekend decisions and complain that help is unavailable. The original agreement never included weekend staffing, and emergency answers need authorized reviewers. Which TWO actions BEST align expectations and improve the service without silently treating new user demand as permission to bypass the existing approval boundary?

options.text: Reduce the measured escalation timer by excluding weekend hours without communicating the measurement change to sponsors or users.
options.why: Changing measurement silently conceals the coverage gap and misaligns expectations.

options.text: Enable autonomous emergency answers on weekends so users experience continuous coverage while reviewers resume normal approvals on Monday.
options.why: It bypasses the required review precisely when authorized reviewers are unavailable.

options.text: Use incident and demand evidence to negotiate revised scope, staffing, approval ownership, and measurable service targets with the accountable stakeholders.
options.why: An expanded SLA requires operational capacity and explicit authority rather than an informal promise.

options.text: Rename the pilot a twenty-four-hour assistant because the software endpoint remains online, keeping the same weekday escalation staffing.
options.why: Endpoint availability is not the promised availability of safe, reviewed resolution.

options.text: Communicate the current coverage and escalation limits clearly in the product and support channels, including the approved route for urgent unsupported situations.
options.why: Users need an honest operating boundary and safe fallback before new coverage is agreed.

questions.decision: New demand is evidence for renegotiation, not automatic scope authorization. Distinguish endpoint uptime, staffed resolution, and required review.

questions.title: A diagram is not a handoff contract
questions.stem: A document assistant passes its pilot and is transferred to a platform team. The receiving team has the architecture diagram but cannot determine which changes require re-evaluation, who owns source freshness, or how to disable unsafe answers. The project is now preparing handoff rather than selecting its initial design. Which deliverable BEST closes the documented operational gap without merely repeating the component picture?

options.text: Ask the original developer to remain informally available for questions, avoiding written procedures that could become stale after future changes.
options.why: Personal availability is fragile and does not create a tested, accountable transfer of service operation.

options.text: Provide versioned interfaces and configurations, acceptance gates, source-refresh ownership, incident and rollback runbooks, and a tested transfer with named receiving owners.
options.why: It turns the design into an operable service with change controls and assigned responsibilities.

options.text: Prepare an executive value presentation describing pilot accuracy and expected capacity benefits, treating positive pilot results as sufficient operational guidance.
options.why: Business value evidence cannot replace runbooks, configuration detail, or ownership at handoff.

options.text: Add more component icons and network arrows to the existing diagram, leaving operational ownership to be inferred from team names.
options.why: More topology does not define change gates, source freshness responsibility, or unsafe-answer response.

questions.decision: Handoff evidence must enable the receiving team to operate, change, and recover the system. A diagram explains structure but not sufficient operational responsibility.

questions.title: A release that is not ready to be owned
questions.stem: A pilot has met quality gates, but its original team will leave next month. Operations has not practiced rollback, the source-data owner has not accepted freshness responsibility, and the support team cannot distinguish model failures from upstream outages. The sponsor wants production next week. Which THREE actions BEST support the current handoff phase while preserving the already demonstrated pilot value and avoiding a premature broad release?

options.text: Have the receiving operations team rehearse rollback and incident diagnosis against realistic failure cases using the documented configuration and approved recovery controls.
options.why: A rehearsal establishes actual operational ability rather than only possession of documents.

options.text: Assign and confirm source-freshness ownership, refresh monitoring, and escalation behavior when required evidence is outdated or unavailable.
options.why: Freshness responsibility must survive departure of the pilot team.

options.text: Agree explicit handoff acceptance criteria and an accountable go-live decision, identifying remaining readiness gaps and a controlled release scope where justified.
options.why: Named acceptance makes the outstanding operational risks visible and governs whether launch is defensible.

options.text: Restart discovery from the beginning and discard all pilot evidence because the original implementation team will no longer operate the service.
options.why: The gap is handoff readiness, not proof that the established need and pilot results are invalid.

options.text: Declare handoff complete because the pilot already passed quality gates, leaving operations to learn recovery during the first production incident.
options.why: Pilot correctness does not demonstrate receiving-team readiness or effective recovery.

questions.decision: The phase determines the missing evidence. Preserve valid pilot work while requiring accountable readiness, transfer of ownership, and practiced recovery before broad operation.

questions.title: The first unresolved lifecycle question
questions.stem: A bank has an approved plan to test a document-summary assistant, but pilot users now request automatic credit-limit recommendations. The current sponsor can authorize summaries; a separate credit-risk committee governs limit decisions. Engineers could add the feature quickly using existing data. Which next action BEST handles this requested capability at the correct lifecycle boundary instead of treating it as an ordinary prompt refinement within the existing pilot?

options.text: Add the recommendation field to the summary prompt and use the existing pilot’s positive summary ratings as evidence that the feature is safe.
options.why: Ratings of summaries do not validate credit decisions or extend the sponsor’s authority.

options.text: Scope the new capability with credit-risk and business owners, establishing authority, intended use, evidence, and acceptance conditions before design.
options.why: Automatic credit recommendations introduce a different decision scope and governing owner that the summary pilot did not authorize.

options.text: Prepare a handoff runbook for the recommendation feature immediately, assuming the credit-risk committee can review its business implications after launch.
options.why: Handoff is premature while the capability’s authority, intended use, and acceptance conditions remain unresolved.

options.text: Treat the request as operational iteration because the existing assistant already has access to the information needed to produce a credit recommendation.
options.why: Data access does not authorize a new consequential decision function or establish its requirements.

questions.decision: A material new decision boundary can require renewed discovery even inside an existing project. Technical feasibility and data access do not settle authority.

questions.title: Averages cannot promise a tail SLA
questions.stem: A provider quotes average model response time of 0.8 seconds. The customer’s target is p95 completed user response below four seconds, including retrieval, authorization, external inventory checks, and generation. No representative end-to-end load test exists yet, and the inventory service slows at peak demand. Which TWO actions BEST support a credible commitment and an informed discussion with the customer?

options.text: Explain current evidence limits and agree provisional targets, dependency ownership, fallback behavior, and acceptance tests before promising the final service level.
options.why: It aligns expectations with measured readiness and makes operational dependencies accountable.

options.text: Exclude the inventory check from the customer-visible timer because it is operated by a different team and cannot be optimized by the architect.
options.why: The user’s completed response still depends on the check; team ownership does not remove it from the promised outcome.

options.text: Promise the four-second SLA because the quoted model average leaves more than three seconds for all other components under normal conditions.
options.why: Averages do not establish tail budgets or peak dependency behavior.

options.text: Add the published average latency of each component and report the sum as p95 for the complete workflow in the contract.
options.why: The sum of averages is not a measured p95, and component tails may be dependent.

options.text: Measure the complete authorized workflow under representative load and data slices, reporting p95 completion and dependency contributions rather than the model average alone.
options.why: The commitment concerns an end-to-end tail, including the slow external dependency.

questions.decision: A service commitment must match the measured system and percentile. Explain uncertainty and ownership before committing to a tail target inferred from averages.

questions.title: An architecture decision survives changed assumptions
questions.stem: A team chose direct document context over retrieval because the approved corpus was small, stable, and uniformly accessible. Six months later it has hundreds of documents with per-department access and frequent revisions. New engineers find the old diagram but no reason for the original choice. Which documentation and lifecycle response BEST supports an evidence-based revision without treating either the old architecture or a fashionable replacement as automatically correct?

options.text: Document only the new component diagram after implementation, leaving decision rationale out because future teams can infer it from selected technologies.
options.why: That repeats the very gap preventing informed reassessment of the original decision.

options.text: Replace the direct-context design with agents immediately because the corpus now has more documents than a person could reasonably read manually.
options.why: Corpus growth alone does not determine the best orchestration or retrieval design and ignores access and latency requirements.

options.text: Record the original decision’s assumptions, constraints, evidence, and revisit triggers, then evaluate alternatives against the changed corpus, access, freshness, and service requirements.
options.why: It connects the previous choice to its conditions and makes a revision testable under the new workload.

options.text: Keep the existing architecture because a production diagram implies the design was approved permanently and changes would invalidate earlier pilot evidence.
options.why: Approval applied to a context; changed assumptions can require a new decision without erasing prior evidence.

questions.decision: Architectural decisions should retain the conditions under which they were justified. Changed conditions trigger evaluation, not blind loyalty or automatic replacement.

questions.title: Project instructions are not a permissions boundary
questions.stem: A team adopts Claude Code and places a rule in its project instructions forbidding production database mutations. The shell environment still contains a production credential capable of writes, and a developer assumes the instruction guarantees enforcement. The team needs a setup that remains safe if the model misinterprets a task. Which configuration change BEST addresses the gap while retaining useful development and staging access?

options.text: Store the production credential in an ignored local file so it is absent from version control but still available to every generated shell command.
options.why: Ignoring a file protects repository distribution, not the running assistant’s capability to use the credential.

options.text: Repeat the production-write prohibition at the top and bottom of project instructions, relying on extra emphasis to establish the required enforcement.
options.why: Repeated instructions remain model context and do not revoke accessible production write authority.

options.text: Remove production write credentials from the development environment and enforce allowed operations through scoped permissions and appropriate controls, keeping project instructions for workflow guidance.
options.why: Removing authority and enforcing capabilities address the risk independently of instruction compliance.

options.text: Require Claude Code to summarize the prohibition at session startup, treating a correct summary as proof that production writes cannot occur.
options.why: Understanding or restating a rule is not a technical capability boundary.

questions.decision: Separate helpful project context from enforced permissions. An instruction cannot revoke an available credential; remove unnecessary authority at the environment boundary.

questions.title: A reproducible team coding workflow
questions.stem: A team finds that AI-generated changes pass on one engineer’s machine but fail in CI. Different developers provide different build commands, and generated patches sometimes skip required integration checks. The repository already has reliable CI commands and a documented review process. Which TWO improvements BEST make AI-assisted work reproducible without duplicating the build system or treating generated test claims as sufficient evidence?

options.text: Ask each developer to maintain personal alternative build scripts so their preferred AI workflow can compensate for differences in the shared CI environment.
options.why: Separate scripts create additional drift rather than aligning development with authoritative CI commands.

options.text: Run the existing relevant checks on generated changes and record their real outcomes, retaining human review for architecture and risks the tests cannot cover.
options.why: Actual check execution and review address reproducibility and broader correctness without trusting assertions in generated text.

options.text: Allow the assistant to mark checks passed when it predicts the patch is straightforward, keeping CI reserved for changes written entirely by humans.
options.why: Predicted outcomes are not test evidence, and AI-generated changes still affect the same production behavior.

options.text: Copy all CI configuration into every task prompt and permit generated replacements when the assistant considers an existing integration check unnecessary.
options.why: Duplicated context becomes stale, and unilateral removal of required checks undermines the established review contract.

options.text: Put concise repository-specific build and review guidance in shared project instructions, referencing the existing authoritative commands and preserving their ownership in version control.
options.why: Shared guidance reduces inconsistent prompts while reusing the project’s actual build and review contract.

questions.decision: Reuse the existing build contract and review process, make it discoverable in shared instructions, and verify actual execution instead of generated assurances.

questions.title: A failed hook is an operational failure
questions.stem: A team uses a pre-execution policy hook to reject prohibited shell operations. After a configuration change, developers report unexplained permission failures on permitted commands. The model’s prompt and tool descriptions are unchanged, and the hook process has started returning malformed output. Which debugging action BEST follows the observed evidence while preserving the control until a validated repair is available?

options.text: Disable all policy hooks for the team and leave them disabled because permitted commands should not depend on an external validation process.
options.why: It removes the required enforcement instead of diagnosing and repairing its documented operational failure.

options.text: Retry every blocked command automatically with broader permissions, counting a successful retry as proof that the original command should have been allowed.
options.why: Broader retries bypass the boundary and do not distinguish valid failures from malformed-hook behavior.

options.text: Inspect the hook execution contract, reproduce allowed and prohibited cases, and deploy a tested repair with bounded diagnostic logging.
options.why: The changed enforcement component and malformed output are the direct evidence; both allow and deny paths need verification.

options.text: Rewrite the system prompt to ask Claude not to mention permissions, assuming the apparent failure is a misunderstanding of the user’s intended command.
options.why: The malformed hook output is an execution-layer problem, not evidence of a prompt misunderstanding.

questions.decision: Diagnose the component that changed using its actual execution contract. Preserve the safety purpose while testing both permitted and prohibited cases after repair.

questions.title: Operational telemetry without source-code capture
questions.stem: A development organization wants to evaluate Claude Code adoption through usage, cost, and workflow bottlenecks across teams. Security prohibits collecting raw proprietary prompts or source files in the central metrics store. The organization can deploy approved telemetry configuration and aggregate operational events. Which approach BEST supports the enablement question while respecting the collection boundary and avoiding a misleading productivity conclusion based solely on token volume?

options.text: Collect approved aggregate usage, costs, and operational events; compare workflow outcomes while excluding prohibited prompt and source content.
options.why: It uses permitted telemetry and relates activity to actual workflow improvement rather than assuming more tokens means more productivity.

options.text: Disable all telemetry because source code is sensitive, then rely on the assistant’s self-reported estimates of developer time saved each week.
options.why: The boundary permits aggregate operational evidence, and self-estimated savings are not independently verified outcomes.

options.text: Rank teams by total generated tokens and assume the highest-volume teams have achieved the largest business productivity improvements.
options.why: Token volume measures activity and can rise with rework; it does not establish productive outcomes.

options.text: Collect all prompts and source patches centrally so managers can manually rate productivity, deleting sensitive details only after reports are generated.
options.why: The collection itself violates the boundary; later deletion does not authorize initial central capture.

questions.decision: Measure permitted operational activity and actual workflow outcomes separately. Data minimization does not require abandoning useful approved aggregate telemetry.

drills.title: Execution and authority checks
drills.stem: Judge each proposal independently against its stated operational obligation. Answer Yes or No for every row; there is no fixed number of Yes answers.

rows.text: Required: approval before publication of uncertain clinical summaries. Proposed: keep them pending when the reviewer timeout expires and invoke the approved staffing fallback.
rows.why: The timeout preserves the pre-publication review requirement and exposes the capacity exception.

rows.text: Required: read-only account assistance. Proposed: retain write credentials but hide write-tool buttons from the chat interface.
rows.why: Hidden interface controls do not revoke the reachable execution capability.

rows.text: Required: prevent duplicate sends after uncertain mail timeouts. Proposed: persist an operation identity and reconcile the external delivery state before retrying.
rows.why: Durable identity and reconciliation address uncertainty about committed external effects.

rows.text: Required: authorize each account read. Proposed: trust any valid company token because all employees authenticate through the same identity provider.
rows.why: Authentication and company membership do not establish account-specific authorization.

rows.text: Required: enforce current project access before the next query. Proposed: filter against current authorization before exposing indexed chunks, even while content refresh is delayed.
rows.why: Current authorization is enforced independently of content-index freshness.

drills.title: Evidence and measurement checks
drills.stem: For each statement, decide whether the conclusion follows from the supplied evidence. Judge every row independently.

rows.text: The new prompt improves average quality but violates an independent critical-slice gate. An improved average alone authorizes broad release.
rows.why: An independent gate cannot be offset by an aggregate gain.

rows.text: A router tests well only on its difficult path. This proves the untested cheap path meets the end-to-end quality requirement.
rows.why: The majority path and routing mistakes still lack relevant evidence.

rows.text: An external booking database confirms the requested change and no unauthorized effects. This supports task-outcome success even if communication quality needs separate review.
rows.why: Outcome and communication are distinct dimensions with different appropriate evidence.

rows.text: The completed-answer p95 target is six seconds. A one-second first token proves compliance even though full answers finish at nine seconds.
rows.why: First-token and completed-answer latency are different metrics.

rows.text: The same policy paragraph appears in development and test paraphrases. Grouping future splits by policy family can reduce that source-level leakage.
rows.why: Grouping protects the evidence boundary rather than merely varying question wording.

drills.title: Select the primary missing artifact
drills.stem: Choose the artifact that most directly fills each described gap. Choices may repeat. These practice categories are not a universal delivery framework.

rows.text: Teams disagree about what an exception means and which business owner may authorize automated rerouting.
rows.why: The gap concerns problem definition and decision authority before choosing a design.

rows.text: New engineers cannot explain why a small stable corpus originally used direct context or when that choice should be revisited.
rows.why: The rationale, assumptions, and revisit triggers belong with the architectural decision.

rows.text: The receiving team has never rehearsed disabling unsafe output or restoring the earlier retrieval configuration.
